# Trust Before Scale: What We’ve Learned Evaluating AI at India’s Largest Private Bank

B *uilding AI has never been cheaper. Proving that it works for every customer, and being able to show why, is still hard. At India’s largest private bank, that proof now decides what goes live.*


A few years ago, building a useful AI system took a specialist team and a long runway. Today any team can pick up a capable model from any vendor, at a falling price, and have a convincing demo in a few weeks.


For a bank, though, the demo was never the difficult part. We run on trust. Customers expect the right answer every time. Regulators expect us to explain how we got there. And leadership has to weigh what AI might save against what it might cost if it goes wrong. A model that’s right most of the time isn’t a product. It’s an unmeasured risk.


As AI spread across the bank, into customer conversations, documents, voice calls and now agents that act for customers, the question in our reviews shifted. People stopped asking whether we could build something and started asking whether we could prove it worked. Answering that one project at a time didn’t scale, so we turned evaluation into a bank-wide capability with a single standard and a single platform. This post is about how we built it and what we learned along the way. If there’s one idea to take away, it’s that in a bank, trust is what lets AI scale.


## The bar every AI system must clear


Every AI system that reaches an HDFC Bank customer has to answer the same five questions:


- **Is it accurate?** Answers grounded in the bank’s own policies and data.
- **Is it private?** Customer information protected in each interaction.
- **Is it fair?** The same quality of service for all customers, whatever their language or background.
- **Is it secure?** Resilient when someone deliberately tries to misuse it.
- **Is it accountable?** Each outcome explainable to a customer, an auditor or a regulator.


For security, we didn’t invent our own rulebook. We follow the[OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/) and the[OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/) , the most widely used catalogues of AI risk. Working from a public standard means our results can be compared and audited, and it keeps us current as new threats get added.


The bar applies throughout a system’s life. Any model that comes into the bank, whether it’s a frontier model, an open-source or Indian-built one, or something we built ourselves, is evaluated before we approve it. Several frontier, open-source and small language models have already been through. Each use case built on top of a model is then evaluated again in its own context before launch, and on a schedule after it. Every stage ends with a decision: approve, approve with conditions, or hold.


> *The platform that does all this is* ***Mulyankan*** *, HDFC Bank’s enterprise AI evaluation platform. It uses one method across conversational assistants, document intelligence, voice and agentic systems, and turns the results into risk ratings our risk functions can review independently. We build AI on NEEV; Mulyankan decides whether it’s ready to go live.*

## How an AI system earns its approval


Here’s a typical case. A team builds an assistant that answers customer questions about account rules. Before it launches, it goes through four steps in Mulyankan.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


**1. Connect.** The assistant plugs into Mulyankan through a standard interface. So can any model, whether frontier, open-source, Indian-built or fine-tuned, and any AI agent. Nobody has to build their own evaluation setup.


**2. Build the evaluation dataset, in context.** Most of the effort goes here, and it’s where generic evaluation tends to fall down. A public benchmark tells you how a model copes with someone else’s questions. Mulyankan starts from the use case instead: it reads the source documents and the assistant’s purpose, then writes the questions real customers are likely to ask, each with the answer the bank expects. It also simulates whole conversations, builds adversarial scenarios mapped to the OWASP risk categories, and evaluates voice systems on call audio. Teams can add their own cases, and systems already in production are evaluated on real interactions.


**3. Score independently.** A separate “challenger” AI model reviews each response on more than 20 dimensions, including accuracy, completeness, hallucination, bias, toxicity, data leakage, jailbreak resistance and the OWASP categories, and writes down why it gave each score. (How we keep that judge honest is the next section.)


**4. Decide.** The risk functions get a report with a score and reasoning for each dimension, the responses that fell short, and a side-by-side comparison with earlier versions or other models.


For our assistant, the report might say it was accurate on eligibility rules, incomplete on reactivation steps, and didn’t expose any customer data. The team fixes the reactivation gap, runs the evaluation again, and walks into the risk review with evidence in hand.


That’s where the time goes back to the team. A hand-written evaluation dataset takes weeks and only covers what its authors thought to ask. A generated one takes a fraction of the time and looks much more like what the system will actually face. Every reviewer reads the same report regardless of which team built the system, and picking between two models becomes a comparison on our own data.


## Who Judges the Judge: The Core Debate Shaping AI Trust


AI-assisted scoring is the only practical way to evaluate at bank scale. Thousands of responses get assessed in hours, work that would take expert teams months. Any risk committee will reasonably ask: if an AI model is doing the assessment, what assures the assessment itself?


Press enter or click to view image in full size


The research community argues about this too. AI judges can be very good. In one landmark study, a leading frontier model agreed with human preferences more than 80% of the time, about as often as humans agree with each other ([Zheng et al., NeurIPS 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685) ). Left to themselves, though, they drift towards leniency, they like confident and lengthy answers, and they prefer their own writing and that of their model family ([Panickssery et al., NeurIPS 2024](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/7f1f0218e45f5414c79c0679633e47bc-Abstract-Conference.html) ;[Li et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.01534) ).


Headline agreement numbers can hide a lot. Even the best judges can be five points off human scores ([Thakur et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12624) ), and on hard questions with objectively correct answers they do only slightly better than chance ([JudgeBench, ICLR 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.12784) ). Outside English it gets worse. Across ten Indian languages and around 90,000 human evaluations, human and AI judges agreed less when asked to score answers directly ([Pariksha, EMNLP 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.15053) ).


> *This is why the field’s most debated question today is:* ***Who checks the checker?*** *Replacing Judges with Juries (*[arXiv 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.18796) *), shows a “jury” of small language models (SLMs) consistently produces* ***higher correlation with human evaluations*** *, reduces systemic bias by drawing from diverse model families, and operates at* ***over seven‑times lower token cost*** *.*


So we treat the judge as one more model that needs governing. Mulyankan puts four constraints on it.


- **The judge labels; rules score.** We don’t ask the judge for a score. We ask narrow questions: is this claim supported by the bank’s source material, contradicted by it, or unsupported? Fixed rules turn those answers into a score, and a material factual error caps it, however polished the rest of the response is.
- **Only the evidence counts.** Responses are checked against the use case’s source material, never the judge’s general knowledge. Style, length and fluency earn nothing, and the same standard applies in any language, including mixed-language replies.
- **The judge gets validated too.** Its instructions are calibrated on cases where we already know the right outcome, before first use and again before any change ships.
- **When it’s unsure, a person looks.** If the judge can’t reach a confident verdict, the case goes to a human reviewer.
- **Diversified judgment** . Building on emerging research — especially work showing that “LLM juries” outperform single frontier judges in both stability and cost — *Mulyankan* will evolve to support *panel‑based evaluation* .


Each result shows the specific finding and the evidence for it, so reviewers can challenge the reasoning itself. We get coverage of every response, and our experts spend their time only where they’re needed.


## Finding weaknesses before attackers do


Accuracy tells you how a system behaves when customers use it as intended. A bank also has to know what happens when someone doesn’t. Sooner or later, every customer-facing AI system meets a person trying to pull out data, override its instructions or push it past its mandate. We’d much rather find those weak spots ourselves.

Mulyankan has a built-in adversarial evaluation capability, essentially an automated red team. It writes attacks tailored to the use case, runs them against the real system and scores how well the system holds up.


**What it tries to make the system do.** Each attack aims at something with real consequences for a bank:


- **Expose customer data** to someone not entitled to it.
- **Reveal its internal instructions** and configuration.
- **Exceed its authority** by acting beyond its mandate.
- **Mislead with confidence** on rates, fees or eligibility.
- **Treat customers unequally** through biased or toxic responses.
- **Assist wrongdoing** , such as fraud.
- **Act against the bank’s interests** by endorsing competitors or reproducing protected content.


**How it attacks.** The same ways a determined adversary would:


- **Direct manipulation:** injected instructions, role-play personas and assumed insider knowledge.
- **Disguise:** harmful requests hidden in encoded text, another language or an innocent-looking task.
- **Persistence:** multi-turn conversations that refine, escalate or branch until the system gives way.


**Built for agents, anchored to OWASP.** Once systems start taking actions, the risks change. Mulyankan’s coverage maps to both OWASP catalogues.


For language-model applications that includes prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, system prompt leakage, excessive agency and misinformation. For agentic systems it includes goal hijacking, tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, memory and context poisoning, and rogue agents.


Every response is scored with a written reason and grouped by risk category, so the risk functions can see where a system holds and where it needs hardening. The bigger change is how often this happens. Red-teaming used to be a scarce, manual exercise kept for the highest-profile systems. In Mulyankan it’s part of every evaluation, and it runs again whenever a model or prompt changes.


## Under the hood: Mulyankan at a glance


All of this runs on one platform. Systems connect once, a governed evaluation core assesses them, and the evidence trail is there for the risk functions, use case teams and leadership to act on.

## **Lessons from the journey, and the road ahead**


Our starting rule was simple enough. Nothing reaches a customer without evidence that it’s ready. Sticking to it, across every model so far and the use cases now being onboarded, changed how we evaluate in ways we didn’t fully expect.


### What the journey taught us


> ***Coverage has to be designed.*** *Early on, our judges chose for themselves which claims to check. Anything they skipped simply never counted, and the results looked better than they should have. Now code picks out every figure and sensitive detail in a response, and the judge has to rule on each one.*
>
>
> ***Real customers broke our assumptions.*** *They interrupt halfway through a sentence. They say “yes” when they mean “go on”. They ask, in two languages at once, whether they’re talking to a machine. Clean, typed test data never showed us any of this, and each case now has its own check.*
>
>
> ***We stopped relying on prompts to enforce rules.*** *We caught judges marking a fact as contradicted and then grading leniently anyway, misreading numbers spoken in Hindi, and now and then reporting values the system never produced. We fixed each one in code. In blind validation afterwards, the judges matched the expected grade in every case. Where they disagreed with our human labellers, it turned out the humans had been too lenient.*
>
>
> ***Evaluation has its own cost line.*** *Judging one voice call used tens of thousands of tokens, about as many as the bot used on the call itself, and nearly four-fifths of that was the bot’s instructions repeated for each check. Caching prompts and asking judges to report only exceptions brought that down sharply without losing any findings. If evaluation costs as much as the system it’s checking, it won’t scale.*
>
>
> ***Same-family judges share blind spots.*** *We saw first-hand what the research describes: on a faint scan, a judge from the same model family as the system accepted values its sibling had misread. Independence is something you have to choose deliberately.*
>
>
> ***Adoption follows zero setup.*** *Our metrics read each system’s rules from its own instructions, so a new bot can be evaluated on day one without any configuration. Reliability mattered just as much. When an 8,000-row experiment froze report generation, fixing scale jumped to the top of the list.*


## The road ahead


Mulyankan has to keep up with AI itself, and the next phase is about broader coverage, cheaper judgements and continuous assurance.


**Deeper attacks, richer datasets.** Banking-specific attack scenarios, longer customer journeys and more Indian languages are next, so coverage keeps pace with how customers and adversaries actually behave.


**Smaller, smarter judges, working as juries.** Many checks, like spotting toxic language or exposed personal data, are well defined and high volume. Inside LLM juries, those can move from large models to specialised classifiers and fine-tuned small language models, for a fraction of the token cost. It’s the same “cost per intelligence” thinking behind our small-model work, applied to evaluation.


**Continuous assurance.** Today, live systems are re-evaluated on a schedule, so drift shows up at the next run. We’re moving to continuous monitoring of production traffic, with drift detection and early warnings that reach the use case team before customers notice anything.


**Agents, end to end.** When an agent does multi-step work, checking its final answer isn’t enough. We’re extending evaluation to the whole path: which tools it picked, in what order, and whether each action stayed within its mandate.


**More standards.** Alongside OWASP, we plan to map our evaluations to the[NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) and[MITRE ATLAS](https://atlas.mitre.org/) , so one body of evidence can answer whichever framework a reviewer works with.


Building AI will keep getting cheaper. Proving it deserves trust will stay hard, and that’s what will decide who gets to scale. For us, that proof is now a permanent part of how AI is built at HDFC Bank, applied to every model and use case, before launch and long after it. That’s what we mean by trust before scale.


*If you’re working on AI evaluation in a regulated industry, we’d like to compare notes.*
